extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and members of the public seeking an overview of the Tennessee Adult Entertainment Act and related litigation
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic summary of the Tennessee Adult Entertainment Act (SB3/HB9/Public Chapter No. 2), describing the bill's text, definitions, penalties, legislative history, public reactions, and ongoing litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'adult cabaret performance' (SB3/HB9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists 'topless dancers, go-go dancers, exotic dancers, strippers, male or female impersonators' as persons featured in 'adult cabaret performance' and described performances that 'appeal to a prurient interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The original bills framed the definition to include persons 'appealing to a prurient interest' (invoking Miller v. California). The enacted Public Chapter No. 2 words the list slightly differently by adding 'or similar entertainers' and removing the 'appeals to a prurient interest' phrasing, instead stating the defined 'cabaret performances' are harmful to minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition scope — public performance and presence of minors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act bans public 'adult cabaret performance' in public or in front of children; Section 2 prevents any 'adult cabaret performance' on public property or in front of 'a person who is not an adult.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to performances on public property and to performances occurring 'in front of' minors; raised questions about what constitutes 'public property' or being 'in front of' a minor in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance location and licensed-establishment exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill would modify Tenn. Code § 7-51-1401 by adding a delineated section for the definition of a performance of adult cabaret, specifically noting the performance would (1) take place outside of an establishment licensed for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text separates performances occurring outside licensed establishments from those within licensed venues; practical effect: non-licensed public performances targeted while licensed adult establishments are treated differently under the code.

rubrics_metrics.name: No intent requirement for covered conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed definition stated the performance would 'not be required to be intended as a performance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That phrasing indicates the statute would cover conduct whether or not the actor intended it as a performance, broadening potential application to incidental or nonperformative acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescission/prevention of permits and licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2 is worded to override § 7-51-1406 so that any existing law permitting the named actions, or any license that had been issued to permit them (such as a permit for a Pride Festival) would be rescinded and would prevent any future licenses or laws from being granted or enacted regarding the named persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: permits/licenses previously allowing events could be nullified; examples in the article cite the potential rescission of Pride Festival permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and criminal classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill lists penalties: a first offense would be considered a Class A Misdemeanor, with each subsequent offense being considered a Class E Felony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with prior § 7-51-1404 (which started penalties as a Class B misdemeanor punishable only by a $500 fine). Under § 40-35-111: Class A misdemeanor allows up to just shy of one year imprisonment, a fine of $2,500, or both; a Class E felony has a mandatory minimum of one year (cannot exceed six years) and jury cannot assess a fine in excess of $3,000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date / temporal application
rubrics_metrics.description: SB3/HB9's Section 3 stated the bills would take effect on July 1, 2023; Public Chapter No. 2 (as signed) states it applies 'to prohibited conduct occurring on or after' April 1, 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The signed law's effective date differs from the introduced bills' language; practitioners/readers should note which text applies when assessing whether specific conduct fell under the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity / Miller prong invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both SB3 and HB9 specifically list the named persons as appealing to 'the prurient interest,' an acknowledgement of Miller v. California (1973).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bills referenced the Miller test for obscenity; the signed Public Chapter removed the 'prurient interest' language and instead labeled the performances harmful to minors. Readers should note the connection to federal obscenity jurisprudence and how statutory wording interacts with constitutional tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness and definitional gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act was criticized for being overly vague; during debate legislators were unsuccessful in defining 'public space' or 'female impersonator.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics (including the ACLU) warned the vague language would allow subjective enforcement by government officials; lack of clear statutory definitions raises Due Process and First Amendment vagueness concerns in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment challenges and injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law was challenged in federal court; on April 1, 2023, Judge Tommy Parker temporarily blocked implementation citing First Amendment concerns; the temporary injunction was changed to a permanent injunction on June 2, 2023 (later appealed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation timeline matters: courts have enjoined enforcement on constitutional grounds in some instances; readers should track injunctive relief status and geographic scope (e.g., Shelby County implications) because enforcement may be paused in parts of the state pending appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff standing as threshold in constitutional challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: On July 18, 2024, a three judge panel on the Sixth Circuit reinstated the law by ruling that the plaintiffs had lacked the standing to sue; the ruling did not address the law's constitutionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing can be dispositive; a ruling for lack of standing leaves the substantive constitutional questions unresolved. Parties seeking relief must establish proper standing to obtain merits review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with and supersession of existing Tennessee statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act's Section 2 specifically mentions § 7-51-1406 with the intent of overriding that section of existing Tennessee law entirely — but only as it respects the named persons; it would supersede § 7-51-1404 regarding penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory drafting is intended to change how prior local/state provisions apply to listed conduct/people; legal analysis should compare prior statutory text and penalty schemes to the new provisions to determine changes in exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of covered persons — 'or similar entertainers' added
rubrics_metrics.description: The law as signed adds the phrase 'or similar entertainers' behind the enumerated list of persons featured in 'adult cabaret entertainment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That addition broadens the statute beyond the explicit list, increasing interpretive uncertainty about which performances fall within the prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and enforcement scope disputes (county/city differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: After injunctions, some local officials (e.g., Blount County DA) interpreted rulings as applying only to specific counties (Shelby County), and separate local lawsuits and rulings (e.g., Murfreesboro ordinance litigation) produced varying outcomes and settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local prosecutorial positions and federal court orders result in a patchwork of enforcement risk; event organizers and venues must consider county-specific rulings, DA guidance, and pending injunctions when planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil remedies, litigation strategies, and public-interest defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple civil suits were filed (e.g., Friends of George's v. State of Tennessee; ACLU actions); courts issued injunctions, and advocacy groups and performers organized defenses and funds (e.g., Drag Defense Fund).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncriminal relief (injunctions, declaratory judgments) and public-interest litigation strategies have been central to contesting the law; plaintiffs, defenders, and third-party donors have influenced legal and practical outcomes.
